title: Context Engineering & Guardrails
tagline: Write the constraint file that keeps an AI agent inside scope during real build work.
intro: When an engineer runs an AI coding agent at Level 3 (agentic, with approval checkpoints) or Level 4 (more autonomous), the agent doesn't work off tribal knowledge — it works off whatever's written down. That written-down file is where a PM's judgment gets encoded, and increasingly, PMs are the ones best positioned to write it. For an MCP-based agent specifically, the strongest guardrail isn't a sentence telling it not to do something — it's simply never giving it the tool to do that thing at all. The same pattern applies whether the agent is touching onboarding, ACA reporting, or any other regulated Employer Services workflow: the constraints are a product decision before they're an engineering one.

diagram.caption: The autonomy ladder. The higher the level, the more the PM's job shifts from writing tickets to writing the bounds — allowed actions, forbidden actions, escalation rules — the agent operates inside.

scenario.context: Engineering is ready to build the Onboarding Packet Agent using an AI coding agent running at Level 3 (it can write and test code across multiple files, but a human approves before anything merges). The agent itself — the one HR reps will talk to — will run as an MCP client with a small, deliberately limited set of tools.
scenario.brief: Before the engineering team starts building, they've asked you — the PM — to write two things that sit alongside the code: the guardrail file that constrains the coding agent, and the tool boundary that constrains the Onboarding Packet Agent itself once it's live. This is what both agents read before they take any action.

sections.heading: Project context
sections.learning: What is this system, in plain terms, with no assumed prior knowledge? This section sets the stage for everything after it — every other section only makes sense once the agent knows what it's actually working on.

example.text: This system lets an HR rep at Meridian Logistics request, in plain language, that a standard six-document onboarding packet be sent to a set of new hires. It looks up matching new hires, shows the HR rep the match for confirmation, and sends the packet. It does not decide who to hire, does not complete any form on an employee's behalf, and does not touch pay, benefits, or HRIS records beyond looking up name, site, start date, and employment type.

sections.pitfall: Writing context so generic it could describe any HR tool. 'This sends onboarding forms' doesn't tell the agent it must never complete a form on someone's behalf, or that it can only read three specific fields from HRIS — without that, the agent has no way to infer its own boundaries from the project description alone.

sections.heading: Allowed actions
sections.learning: What's explicitly in scope — and for an MCP-based agent, the strongest version of this isn't a sentence, it's the literal set of tools it's given. An agent with no delete_employee_record tool cannot delete an employee record, no matter what anyone asks it to do. Scoping the tool list is the guardrail; everything else is a second layer on top of it.

example.text: lookup_new_hires(criteria) — read-only, returns name, site, start date, employment type. send_packet(employee_id, forms[]) — sends the standard packet, only after HR rep confirmation. check_completion_status(employee_id) — read-only. Nothing else is exposed to this agent.

sections.pitfall: Trying to control scope entirely through prompt instructions ('please don't modify pay records') instead of tool scoping. A prompt instruction can be argued around by a clever enough request; a tool that was never given to the agent cannot be called, period.

field.label: Your turn: Allowed actions
field.help: What tools is the agent given, and what does each one do?
field.placeholder: List the tools, what they return or do, and any behavior required around them.

sections.heading: Forbidden actions
sections.learning: Tool scoping handles what the agent structurally cannot do. Forbidden actions cover the second layer: behaviors that are technically possible with the tools it has, but must never happen anyway — this is where compliance rules that don't map neatly onto a missing tool belong.

example.text: Never call send_packet without first showing the HR rep the matched list and receiving confirmation. Never include an employee's Self-Identification of Disability or Self-Identification as a Protected Veteran responses in any output the HR rep sees — those responses are voluntary and confidential under OFCCP rules, must be kept in a separate file from the rest of the onboarding record, and must never be visible to anyone involved in employment decisions. Never treat a form as completed or verified — completion is confirmed by the employee, not the agent.

sections.pitfall: Writing forbidden actions only for what feels risky in the abstract, and missing the specific compliance trap. Showing self-ID disability or veteran responses in a routine 'here's what's been submitted' status view feels like helpful transparency — it's actually a real confidentiality violation the moment that view is visible to an HR rep who's also involved in hiring decisions.

field.label: Your turn: Forbidden actions
field.help: What must the agent never do, even with the tools it has?
field.placeholder: List the hard no's, as concretely as possible.

sections.heading: Escalation rules
sections.learning: What situations should stop the agent and require a human decision? This is the same discipline that governs any regulated Employer Services flow — an ACA reporting assistant, for instance, would need its own explicit escalation rule for anything touching a filing deadline.

example.text: Any request with an ambiguous date range (e.g., 'next month' issued near a month boundary). Any matched new hire missing a required field (site, start date, employment type). Any employment type the agent hasn't been given packet rules for (the standard six-document packet assumes a first-time employee hire — a rehire or contractor needs a human to confirm which forms apply). Any send_packet call that fails to deliver.

sections.pitfall: Writing escalation rules that only cover missing data, and missing the ones tied to who the packet is even for. A rehire or contractor getting the full standard packet isn't a delivery failure — it's the agent guessing at a case its rules never covered.

field.label: Your turn: Escalation rules
field.help: What situations should stop the agent and require a human decision?
field.placeholder: List the trigger conditions for stopping and asking a human.

sections.heading: Definition of done
sections.learning: How would anyone — human or agent — know this work is actually finished and safe to ship?

example.text: The agent only ever calls its three named tools. Every send_packet call in the historical test set was preceded by a shown, confirmed match. No test case shows a self-ID disability or veteran response anywhere in HR-rep-facing output. Ambiguous-date and non-standard-employment-type test cases all escalate instead of guessing.

sections.pitfall: Defining done as 'the code runs without errors.' That's a technical bar, not a compliance one — done means the confidentiality and confirmation-before-send rules pass on every test case, not just the cases where the request was unambiguous.

field.help: How would anyone know this work is actually finished and safe to ship?
